newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China assures no mass PLA march into HK in 97 - UK.
newsitem.headline: China assures no mass PLA march into HK in 97 - UK.

text.p: Britain's chief of defence staff said on Monday he was assured on a recent visit to China that Beijing would not march large numbers of troops into Hong Kong when it takes over the colony next year.
Field Marshal Sir Peter Inge said he was given a "clear message" during a visit to Beijing last week during which he met People's Liberation Army (PLA) Chief of General Staff Fu Quanyou.

"I was given a very clear message that it was unthinkable that large numbers of PLA troops would march into Hong Kong," Inge, the most senior British military visitor to China since 1989, said in a luncheon speech.
"It was made very clearly to me and I think it showed a sensitivity they felt towards the situation," he said.

The Financial Times of London said last month 6,000 PLA troops would march across the border into Hong Kong, a British colony for more than a century and a half, when it reverts to China on July 1 next year.
Senior military Chinese officials have slammed the report as unfounded.

The arrival of the PLA is viewed with trepidation in Hong Kong where the image of Chinese troops cracking down on the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in June 1989 remains etched in the collective memory.
A unit of the PLA to replace the British garrison has been formed over the border, and a small advance party is expected to arrive before the handover to help with logistics.
Talks between Britain and China on Monday on the deployment of the PLA advance party were deadlocked, participants said.

Representatives of the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group (JLG), the diplomatic body handling Hong Kong's sovereignty transfer, said after the meeting that more negotiations were needed to thrash out differences.
"We haven't made as much progress as I would have liked to have seen but we have agreed that this is an important subject," Alan Paul, British representative to the JLG, told reporters.
"We must continue our efforts and we must meet more often on this subject," Paul said.
Chinese representative Chen Zuo'er blamed differences in army structure, government-funded radio reported.

Britain last week announced a draft bill that would make subversion and sedition crimes in Hong Kong only if they entailed violence, making clear mere dissident-style criticism of the authorities was not a crime.

China promptly denounced the move, arguing it would only bring instability and disruption to Hong Kong, and insisting that only the post-handover government had the right to decide on the legislation.
